claims.text: A pull request names a source branch and a target branch and proposes the merge; opening one does not perform the merge.
claims.source_hint: GitHub Docs, Pull requests — About pull requests

claims.text: Git supplies the branch and the merge locally; the team's shared copy of the repository sits on a hosting service, and the pull request page carrying the diff, the comments and the approval is supplied by that service, not by Git itself.
claims.source_hint: git-scm.com/docs full command list (no review or approval command); GitHub Docs, About pull request reviews

claims.text: Teams give three reasons for code review: finding defects, moving knowledge in both directions between author and reviewer, and keeping the codebase consistent. Treating defects as the only purpose is what makes a review feel like an exam.
claims.source_hint: outline item 1 of the lesson entry in content/tracks/management/track.yaml

claims.text: On a team that grades comments this way, a must-fix holds the merge; a suggestion, question or praise does not. A hosting service can require an approval before a merge, and a reviewer can mark a whole review as still needing changes, but a single comment's grade means nothing to the service.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/review-comments-examples.md lines 7, 11, 14, 18; GitHub Docs: About pull request reviews (Request changes), About protected branches (required approvals)

claims.text: A question asks before it asserts because the reviewer may have misread; by itself it says nothing is wrong, though the author still owes it an answer. Of the note's grades it is the lightest: it holds nothing.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/review-comments-examples.md lines 7-9 and 14-16, both of which ask rather than assert

claims.text: Approval means the change may merge, not that it cannot be improved; when a reviewer holds a change for preferences they could have marked as suggestions, others keep merging into the target branch and the waiting branch collects conflicts.
claims.source_hint: outline item 3 of the lesson entry in content/tracks/management/track.yaml

claims.text: At stage-0, docs/team/story-example.md writes the cancel-order criteria (criterion 3: the Cancel button is not shown for paid, shipped or cancelled orders) and lists a team Definition of Done whose first two entries are: read and approved by at least one other person; a test for every criterion.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docs/team/story-example.md at stage-0, lines 8-24 (criterion 3 at lines 14-15)

claims.text: At stage-0 part of the team's standard is on paper: the story's acceptance criteria, the Definition of Done, and this note on how a comment is phrased. What no file states is the judgement behind them — is this name clear here, which exception to catch — which shows up only in review comments.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4; examples/don-hang docs/team/ at stage-0: story-example.md (criteria, DoD) and review-comments-examples.md (comment wording) are written; no file states naming or exception judgement

claims.text: The author writes the pull request description; when it does not say why the change exists, the reviewer has only the diff to infer intent from.
claims.source_hint: outline item 2 of the lesson entry in content/tracks/management/track.yaml

claims.text: On the service hosting the repository, a pull request is tied to its source branch rather than to a fixed set of commits: commits added to that branch after the pull request is opened appear in the same pull request.
claims.source_hint: GitHub Docs, About pull requests — the Commits tab shows how the pull request branch changed over time

claims.text: A junior who reviews other people's changes reads more changes than they write and sees other reviewers' comments on them, so meets the team's unwritten judgement sooner than one who only receives review.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4 of the lesson entry in content/tracks/management/track.yaml
